name: BCG
summary: BCG's interviews for client-facing roles centre on case interviews, which BCG says judge how you structure and reason through a realistic business problem rather than whether you reach one right answer. Its careers site describes a skills interview on your experience and motivation, a case interview and a team interview, and names the qualities its consulting interviewers look for: integrity, intellectual curiosity, creative thinking, a collaborative mindset and drive.
rounds: Online application, with an online test or online case for some offices and roles
Skills interview on your experience, skills and motivation
Case interviews: a realistic business problem worked through with the interviewer
Team interview for client-facing roles, again on problem solving, analysis and communication
looks_for: Structuring a problem and stating assumptions
Quick, accurate calculations and reading data
Clear communication and a summary that ends in a recommendation

questions.text: Tell me about yourself and what brings you to consulting.
covers: Your background in two or three lines, focused on what's relevant
One achievement that shows how you solve problems
What draws you to consulting now

questions.text: Tell me about a time curiosity made you dig further into a problem than you needed to.
covers: What caught your interest and why you kept going
What you found that others had missed
How it changed the result or your thinking

questions.text: Tell me about a time you came up with an unusual solution to a problem.
covers: The problem and why the usual approaches didn't work
Your idea and how you tested it
The outcome and what you learnt about creative problem solving

questions.text: Describe a time you helped a team work better together.
covers: What wasn't working and how it showed
What you did to change it, including listening to others
How the team's results improved

questions.text: Tell me about the achievement you're proudest of. What drove you?
covers: Why it was hard and what was at stake for you
What you did, in the first person, over time
The result and why it matters to you

questions.text: A coffee chain's new stores are less profitable than its older ones. How would you find out why?
covers: Comparing revenue (footfall, spend per visit) and costs (rent, staff, supplies) between old and new stores
Checking location, store age and local competition before blaming execution
The likely cause and what the chain should do about future openings

questions.text: A car maker is deciding whether to launch a subscription service for its electric cars. How would you assess it?
covers: Who would subscribe and why, compared with buying or leasing
Revenue per subscriber against the costs of cars, servicing and lower resale values
Risks, a recommendation, and a small pilot to test demand

questions.text: Estimate the yearly demand for school notebooks in Bengaluru. Talk me through your assumptions.
covers: Starting from the number of school pupils, by age group
Notebooks per pupil per year, with round numbers you say out loud
A final figure, a sense check, and the assumption that matters most

questions.text: A client's costs are 70% of revenue, and it wants its margin up by 5 points next year with flat revenue. Roughly how much must costs fall, and where would you look?
covers: The maths: costs must go from 70 to 65, a cut of about 7%
The biggest cost areas first, then quick wins versus structural changes
Whether the target is realistic, and the risks of cutting too fast

questions.text: A software company can enter one of three new countries first. How would you decide which?
covers: Criteria: market size and growth, competition, ease of entry, fit with the product
Rough numbers for each country and how they compare
A clear choice, the main risk, and what you'd check first

questions.text: For a technology role: how would you help a retailer decide whether to build its own recommendation engine or buy one?
covers: What the retailer needs: scale, speed, control over data and customer experience
Cost, time and skills to build versus licence cost and limits of buying
A recommendation, often starting small, and how success would be measured
What you want from consulting work, shown by something you've done
Something specific about BCG you learnt from its people, work or events
How it fits your longer-term goals

questions.text: What would you want to learn in your first year here, and how would you know you're growing?
covers: Two or three specific skills you want to build
The kind of projects or industries you'd seek out
How you'd use feedback to track your progress

tips: BCG's case guidance asks you to clarify assumptions, show your thinking and summarise your recommendation at the end; practise all three out loud.
Don't force a memorised framework onto the case; build a structure for the specific problem in front of you.
If the interviewer nudges you mid-case, take it, adjust, and say how it changes your thinking.
Prepare a story for each quality BCG lists: integrity, curiosity, creative thinking, collaboration and drive.
BCG offers a free job simulation, OneDay@BCG, on its careers site; it's a useful way to see the kind of work cases are based on.
Practise mental maths with percentages and growth rates, and round sensibly as you go.
